verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.68, Star Questions Plus, SAQ 188). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: The rule
lines: Van't Hoff's rule states that for every rise
of 10°C in temperature, the rate of the
metabolic activities of an animal doubles.
steps.why: The rule is one sentence and it holds three numbers — the step of 10°C, the factor of two, and the direction of the change — so all three go into the first line.
common_mistakes: Writing that the rate doubles for every 1°C. The step is 10°C.
Writing that the temperature doubles. It is the RATE of metabolism that doubles.
steps.memory_tip: Ten up, rate times two. Ten down, rate halved.
steps.margin_note: One sentence with both numbers in it. Do not start on Q₁₀ yet.

temperature the rate of the metabolic
So the rule works in both directions.
steps.why: Writing the rule the other way round is a separate mark in this answer because it shows the rule is a relation between temperature and rate, not a one-way effect of heating.
common_mistakes: Writing that cooling stops metabolism. It HALVES the rate for each 10°C fall.
Repeating the first statement in the same direction.
steps.memory_tip: Same rule, mirror image: double going up, half coming down.
steps.margin_note: One sentence, reversed. Two lines are enough.

steps.label: Temperature coefficient Q₁₀
lines: The effect of temperature on the rate of a
reaction is expressed in terms of the
Q₁₀ is the ratio between the rate of the
reaction at X°C and the rate at (X − 10)°C.
steps.why: Q₁₀ is the number that MEASURES the rule, so it must be defined as a ratio of two rates ten degrees apart; a definition without the two temperatures does not say what is being compared.
common_mistakes: Calling Q₁₀ a temperature. It is a RATIO of two reaction rates.
Leaving out the 10°C gap between the two rates being compared.
steps.memory_tip: Q₁₀ is a ratio, so it has no units: the rate now divided by the rate ten degrees colder.
steps.margin_note: Name the coefficient and define it as a ratio with the two temperatures.

lines: In living organisms the value of Q₁₀ is
That is, the rate of metabolism doubles for
This is the same statement as the rule
itself, now written as a number.
steps.why: Closing with the value of about 2.0 ties the coefficient back to the rule, showing they are one statement in two forms — words and a number.
common_mistakes: Giving Q₁₀ a value of 10. The value in living organisms is about 2.
Not linking the value back to the rule. The number 2 IS the doubling.
steps.memory_tip: Q₁₀ of 2 and the word doubles say the same thing.
steps.margin_note: The number first, then one line tying it back to the rule.

insider_note: Q₁₀ is the part of this answer most often left out, and it carries half the marks — define it as a ratio and give its value of about 2.
